interest: This file offers valuable insight into the legal status of enemy alien property rights during World War II, demonstrating how pre-war Japanese legislation (Imperial Ordinance No. 334 of 1926) governing alien land ownership was viewed as technically remaining in force even amidst active hostilities. It highlights the vital role played by neutral diplomatic intermediaries, specifically the Swiss Legation in Tokyo reporting through Bern, in monitoring the juridical and property standing of American nationals in wartime Japan. Furthermore, it illustrates the practical intersection between federal foreign relations and state-level administration, as the Department of State evaluated reciprocal property rights in response to matters concerning the State Land Board of Oregon.
overview: This file consists of an internal Department of State memorandum from the Special Division dated April 28, 1943, concerning the rights of aliens, particularly American citizens, to own and inherit real property in Japan during World War II. Prompted by an underlying matter involving the State Land Board in Salem, Oregon, the memorandum examines whether Japan's 1926 Alien Land Law (Imperial Ordinance No. 334) remained operative during the war, noting communications from the Swiss Legation in Tokyo via Bern indicating that American inheritance rights had not been altered by the conflict except for restrictions within designated fortified or national defense zones. The file also includes a 1984 General Services Administration withdrawal notice (GSA Form 7117) marking the removal of a security-classified document under Justice Department guidelines.

subfiles.about: Internal memorandum discussing the ongoing validity of Japan's 1926 Alien Land Law and American inheritance rights in wartime Japan.
subfiles.from: Special Division, Department of State (D. W. Smith)
subfiles.summary: The Special Division addresses an inquiry involving the State Land Board in Salem, Oregon, regarding alien real property rights under Japanese law. Relying on reports forwarded from the Swiss Legation in Tokyo via Bern, the memorandum indicates that the legal position of American citizens regarding inheritance of real and personal property remained unchanged following the declaration of war. It concludes that Japan's Alien Land Law of 1926 (Imperial Ordinance No. 334) appeared to remain operative outside designated fortified defense zones and suggests seeking further confirmation from the Swiss Legation if needed.
